newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian stocks surge on election, rupiah stable.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian stocks surge on election, rupiah stable.

text.p: Indonesian stocks soared on Thursday as the nation voted in general elections, and brokers said the surge was at least partly due to relief that the poll process passed off relatively peacefully.
On the foreign exchange market, trade was thin because many operators took a half-day off to vote. But the rupiah currency was stable and should strengthen, dealers said.

The composite stock index closed 2.53 percent up at 689.5 points, with widespread buying of blue-chips which started on rumours that Singapore Telecom had bought a stake in local market heavyweight PT Telkom.
The buying continued through the day despite a statement by a Telkom official that the company had no plans to place shares with the Singapore firm.
"It was a combination of lots of factors," said Kian Guntur, a trader with PT Schroders Indonesia. "There was the election, Telkom and the fact that there was a lot of programme buying."
"There was a substantial inflow of funds," he added.

The research head of a foreign brokerage, who wanted to remain unnamed, said the Telkom rumour had been floating in the market for a while and added that the end of the election was a more likely cause.
"It is the formal start of post-election buying," he said. "People have been talking about a surge after the elections and it's become a self-fulfilling prophecy."
The research head noted that several companies had announced positive first quarter earnings and the prospects of others doing so could take the index to the 700-point-level next week.

Indonesia's general elections passed off mostly peacefully on Thursday, although 13 people were killed in the troubled territory of East Timor overnight when rebels tried to block the polls process, police said.
One soldier guarding a polling booth was killed in the territory on Thursday, police said.
Brokers and analysts said violence in East Timor rarely affects markets in Jakarta. Fears of instability usually rise if there are widespread clashes on the main island of Java, they added.
The rupiah closed in Jakarta at 2,440.50/40.80 against the dollar from a 2,439/40 open and dealers said trade was quiet.

Desmond Supple, an exotic currencies specialist with BZW Barclays in Singapore, said he expected the rupiah to strengthen over the medium-term but added that trade over the next few days would be choppy.
He said there was no further build-up of long dollar positions, which was much in evidence as violence broke out during the election campaign, but added that there was no aggressive shorting either.
"Event risk has not subsided as yet," he told Reuters. "Investors will be looking for re-entry levels into the rupiah but it is imprudent at the moment to reverse long holdings."
But he added: "Once the results are out, the potential for instability will fall."
Counting had started in several polling stations across the country and the ruling Golkar party seemed assured of a comfortable victory.

Political analysts said there was concern that supporters of Golkar's main rival during the campaign, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP), might stage protests if they did not increase their vote share and felt cheated.
Most of the violence in the campaign has involved street battles between supporters of the PPP and Golkar.
